L	The Economics was far from the only text of antiquity to tackle the question of home. First,
there was Xenophon’s book of the same name, written slightly before Aristotle’s, and slightly
less interesting. And later, Stoic writers took up the topic of the home with some enthusiasm,
writing about marriage, the family and the education of women. The most notable among
them were perhaps Musonius Rufus, a 1st-century CE Roman philosopher, and Hierocles the
Stoic, a 2nd-century CE Greek philosopher. Then there is the whole corpus of texts by a group
of philosophers known as the Neo-Pythagoreans, some signed by women, and many of them
discussing the home, women’s virtues and marital relations. The home, it turns out, was a
topic of considerable philosophical interest in antiquity.
Many of the fragments we have from Neo-Pythagorean writers who sign their texts with
women’s names concern the ethics and politics of domestic arrangements: what to do if your
husband cheats on you? How to deal with household slaves? Would a woman’s virtue enable
her, in principle, to rule a state? These texts are commonly rejected by studies of ancient
philosophers because they are hard to date, and quite likely written by writers using
pseudonyms. But they are philosophical texts written in antiquity, and they are about the
home, and I suspect that, if the home was regarded as a topic worthy of philosophical
interests, they would be read today. The Neo-Pythagorean authors are the subject of several
recent excellent and accessible books — eg, Pythagorean Women (2013) by Sarah Pomeroy,
Pythagorean Women Philosophers (2020) by Dorota Dutsch, PythagoreanWomen (2022) by
Caterina Pellé — so I would urge readers to consult these, and will now turn to Musonius and
Hierocles.
Musonius Rufus had his 15 minutes of fame some 25 years ago when Martha Nussbaum
noticed that he recommended women be educated as well as men. But while education does
matter to gender relations, so does the home, and Musonius, it turns out, has a lot to say about
that, as well as about education. First, he says that marriage is ‘community of life with a view
to the procreation of children’. Then he goes further and explores what married life should be
like, and what its legal and moral implications are. The marital ‘community’, he argues, must
be material and emotional: a husband and wife must regard ‘all things in common between
them, and nothing peculiar or private to one or the other, not even their own bodies.’ As well
as sharing their material possessions, they must share affection: there should be ‘above all
perfect companionship and mutual love of husband and wife’. If these conditions fail to obtain,
‘the union is doomed to disaster and though they live together, yet their common interests fare
badly’. [Word Count: 462]

IV.	Having gone quiet for a few months since lockdown, the reliably informative Exhibition on
Screen series returns with a profile of Frida Kahlo, the Mexican painter who has long been
venerated as a pioneer of feminist iconography as well as a champion of the country’s
indigenous culture. While the series tends to use large-scale exhibitions as a cue, this film
spends only brief periods inside a gallery spaces — primarily the Museo Dolores Olmedo in
Mexico City, which holds significant amounts of Kahlo’s work, as well as her husband’s Diego
Rivera. Instead, we get a straightforward, meat-and-potatoes overview of Kahlo’s life,
peppered with copious commentary from the usual top-notch academic and curatorial talent,
as well as family members.
While it’s perhaps not fair to make grandiose claims for this sober-toned film, I suspect it’s
trying to somehow reclaim the artist from “Fridamania”, the surge of admiration that swept
the cultural world in the 70s and 80s when Kahlo’s preoccupations — her brutal physical
realities, the adoption of costume and imagery, the use of her body as a personal theatre —
became fashionable, decades after her death. There’s a measured tone throughout, as well as
some great photographs: Kahlo with Rivera, who always seems to look as if he’s just woken up;
Kahlo’s father, whose spiffy goatee is surely the source of the shadowy facial hair Kahlo liked
to paint on to herself; and Kahlo herself as a radiant teenager and twentysomething, despite
the horrific bus crash that affected her from the age of 18.
Though necessarily a little light on detail, this is a film that covers the required bases, striking
a good balance between Kahlo’s often dramatic personal life and the ins and outs of her artistic
achievements. (A fervent case is made that Kahlo was the first artist to render menstrual
blood on canvas, in her heartbreaking depiction of her miscarriage and hospital stay in
Detroit, where she had accompanied Rivera on one of his mural commissions.)
There’s also an interesting sidebar on Mexican retablo painting — the votive street art that is
still a traditional method of attempting to gain divine intercession — which Kahlo herself
collected and which was a clear influence on her own work. All in all, a very watchable film
about an ever-intriguing figure. [Word Count: 376]

V.	With global temperatures at near-record levels and El Nifio set to return, governments,
businesses, communities, and individuals across the world today marked World Environment
Day, sounding the alarm on the need to urgently address climate change. This year,
Azerbaijan hosted the official commemoration of World Environment Day.
Extreme heat is one of the deadliest and fastest-growing climate threats to lives, livelihoods,
and economies. The overshoot of the Paris Agreement goal of 1.5°C now almost inevitable and
impacts escalating, cutting emissions and adapting to rising risks.
This World Environment Day, warning signals are everywhere. The past eleven years have
been the eleven hottest on record. The world is heading for a temporary overshoot above 1.5
degrees, UN Secretary-General Anténio Guterres stated in his message for World
Environment Day 2026. Our task is to make that overshoot as small, as short, and as safe as
possible — and rapidly bring temperatures back down.
That means slashing emissions. Accelerating a just transition away from fossil fuels and
towards renewables — the only sustainable path to lower costs and to real energy security.
Cutting methane — one of the fastest, cheapest ways to limit near-term warming. Protecting
forests, land, and seas. Helping communities adapt to the devastating impacts already here.
And it means fulfilling climate finance promises to developing countries — to save lives, protect
livelihoods, and strengthen economies, he added. This is the moment to act — for our
environment and for our future. As our planet continues to face the devastating impacts of
climate change, the science is clear. [Word Count: 252]

mortgage, charge, sell, gift, exchange, or otherwise transfer any part of the minor’s immovable

accrue to the minor rather than focusing solely on technical objections.

stationary autorickshaw could be treated as an accident “arising out of the use of a motor

it and caused grievous injuries, including permanent paraplegia.
The main provision considered was Section 165 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. This section
empowers the State Government to constitute Motor Accident Claims Tribunals for deciding
compensation claims arising from accidents involving death, bodily injury, or damage to third-
party property. However, the accident must arise out of the use of a motor vehicle. Therefore,
the Tribunal’s jurisdiction depends not merely on the presence of a vehicle, but on a real
connection between the injury and the use of that vehicle. Section 166 of the Act provides the
procedural route for filing an application for compensation in such cases. A claim under this
section must relate to an accident of the kind described in Section 165. Hence, where the
injury is caused by an external event having no proximate connection with the vehicle’s
movement, operation, condition, or use, Section 166 may not be the proper remedy. The Court
acknowledged that the expression “use of a motor vehicle” has been interpreted broadly. It can
include cases where the vehicle is stationary and not moving. Similarly, the phrase “arising
out of” is wider than “caused by” and does not always require a direct causal connection. Still,
the Court clarified that some proximate and meaningful connection with the vehicle must
exist. In the present case, the autorickshaw merely happened to be the place where the
claimant was sitting. The injury was caused by the falling branch, not by the vehicle.

XII. Wrongful restraint and wrongful confinement are offences against personal liberty and
freedom of movement. Article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution protects the right of citizens to move
freely throughout India, while Article 21 protects personal liberty. Criminal law gives effect to
these guarantees by punishing unlawful obstruction or detention. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023, wrongful restraint is dealt with under Section 126 and wrongful confinement
under Section 127.
Wrongful restraint occurs when a person voluntarily obstructs another person so as to prevent
that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed. The
obstruction may be physical, verbal, threatening, or created by circumstances, provided it
unlawfully prevents movement. The essence of the offence is that the victim must have a legal
right to move in that direction, and the accused must voluntarily obstruct that movement.
Mere advice, request, or moral pressure will not amount to wrongful restraint unless it
effectively prevents lawful movement.
The law also recognises an exception. If a person, in good faith, believes that he has a lawful
right to obstruct a private way over land or water, such obstruction does not amount to
wrongful restraint. However, the belief must be genuine and connected with a private way;
obstruction of a public road or obstruction without lawful basis cannot claim this protection.

when a person wrongfully restrains another in such a manner as to prevent that person from
proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits. In wrongful restraint, movement is blocked
only in one or some directions; in wrongful confinement, the person is prevented from moving
beyond a fixed boundary. Thus, all wrongful confinement involves restraint, but every

XIII. The doctrine of colourable legislation is an important constitutional principle used to examine
whether a legislature has acted within the limits of its law-making power. It is based on the
maxim that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. A legislature may appear
to make a law within its authority, but if the real substance of the law enters a field beyond its
constitutional competence, the law may be treated as colourable legislation.
In India, legislative powers are distributed mainly through Articles 245 and 246 of the
Constitution and the Seventh Schedule. Article 245(1) provides that, subject to the
Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India, and a State
Legislature may make laws for the whole or any part of that State. Article 245(2) provides that
a law made by Parliament shall not be invalid merely because it has extra-territorial
operation.
Article 246 deals with the subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and State Legislatures.
Article 246(1) gives Parliament exclusive power to make laws on matters in List I, known as
the Union List. Article 246(2) allows both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on
matters in List III, known as the Concurrent List. Article 246(3) gives State Legislatures
exclusive power to make laws on matters in List II, known as the State List, subject to
Parliament’s powers under clauses (1) and (2). Article 246(4) allows Parliament to legislate for
any part of India not included in a State, even on matters in the State List.
If a legislature makes a law on a subject assigned to another legislature, it acts beyond its
competence. The doctrine prevents a legislature from disguising such an encroachment by
giving the law an appearance of validity. Courts do not depend merely on the title, form, or
language of the law. They examine the true nature, object, and effect of the legislation.
If the substance of the law falls within the legislature’s field, the law is valid even if it
incidentally affects another field. However, if the substance of the law belongs to an
unauthorised field, it cannot be saved merely because its wording appears lawful.
Colourable legislation is sometimes described as a fraud on the Constitution. This does not
mean dishonest intention. In constitutional law, the focus is on legislative competence, not
personal motive. If the legislature has no power to enact a law, its intention or policy reason
cannot make the law valid. [Word Count: 409]

XIV. Bailment is a special contract recognised under Sections 148 to 171 of the Indian Contract Act,
1872. Section 148 defines bailment as delivery of goods by one person to another for some
purpose, upon a contract that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned
or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. The person
delivering the goods is called the bailor, and the person receiving them is called the bailee.
The essence of bailment is delivery of possession, not transfer of ownership. The bailee
receives temporary possession and must use the goods only for the agreed purpose. Bailment
may arise through express contract, implied contract, or even by operation of law, such as
where a person finds goods belonging to another and assumes responsibility over them.
Section 149 recognises that delivery may be made by doing anything which has the effect of
putting the goods in the possession of the intended bailee.
The bailor has important duties. Under Section 150, the bailor must disclose faults in the
goods which are known to him and which materially interfere with their use or expose the
bailee to extraordinary risk. If the bailor fails to disclose such faults, he is responsible for
damage caused to the bailee. In gratuitous bailment, this duty applies to known faults; in non-
gratuitous bailment, the responsibility is stricter.
The bailee must take reasonable care of the goods. Section 151 requires the bailee to take as
much care of the goods as a person of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods. Under
Section 152, if such care is taken, the bailee is not responsible for loss, destruction, or
deterioration of the goods, unless there is a special contract. However, under Sections 153 and
154, unauthorised use of the goods may terminate the bailment and make the bailee liable for
loss arising from such use.
The bailee must return or deliver the goods according to the bailor’s directions when the
purpose is accomplished or the time of bailment expires. Under Section 161, if the bailee

‘need’ it — but they don’t need it in the same way that they need water or food. Their survival isn’t

Your intellectual appetites might include knowing the answer to a mathematics problem; the
satisfaction of receiving a text from someone you have a crush on; or getting a coveted job offer.
These things won’t necessarily cause physical pleasure. They might spill over into physical
enjoyment, but they are not dependent on it. Rather, the pleasure is primarily intellectual. The
18th-century philosopher and theologian Thomas Aquinas wrote that these intellectual appetites

toward it. If they come to possess the object of their desire, they will find rest in it — and they are
able to experience joy, so long as they are able to rest in the object of their desire.
But, for most people, such joy is fleeting. There is always something else to strive for — and this
keeps most of us in a constant, sometimes painful, state of never-satisfied striving. And that
striving for something that we do not yet possess is called desire. Desire doesn’t bring us joy
because it is, by definition, always for something we feel we lack. Understanding the mechanism by
which desires take shape, though, can help us avoid living our lives in an endless merry-go-round
of desire.
